question_text: A transverse section of the trunk of a tree shows concentric rings, which are known as annual rings. How are these rings formed? What is the significance of these rings?

page_header: Histology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants · 4 marks

steps.label: Spring wood (early wood)
steps.margin_note: Link the season to the leaves, the leaves to the water, the water to the vessels.
lines: The activity of the vascular cambium is not
the same all through the year. It changes with
the season, and in temperate regions the
seasons are sharply marked.
In the favourable season the plant puts out
many leaves and needs a large amount of water.
So the cambium produces secondary xylem with
more vessels and a broader lumen. This wide,
light-coloured wood is spring wood or early
wood.
steps.why: The cambium makes the wood the plant needs at that moment. Many leaves mean heavy water demand, and wide vessels carry more water, so the kind of wood made depends on the season.
common_mistakes: Writing that the cambium stops working in the favourable season. It works fastest then.
Leaving out the vessel width. Broad lumen is what makes spring wood look light.
steps.memory_tip: Many leaves, much water, wide vessels, light wood. That is spring wood.

steps.label: Autumn wood (late wood)
steps.margin_note: Two lines. Keep it as the mirror image of the step above.
lines: In the unfavourable season the plant has few
leaves and needs less water.
So the cambium produces secondary xylem with
fewer vessels and a narrow lumen. This narrow,
dark-coloured wood is autumn wood or late
wood.
steps.why: The same reasoning run backwards: fewer leaves mean less water is needed, so narrow vessels are enough, and closely packed narrow cells look darker.
common_mistakes: Calling autumn wood the wood of autumn only. It is the wood of the whole unfavourable season.
Saying autumn wood has no vessels. It has fewer and narrower ones.
steps.memory_tip: Few leaves, little water, narrow vessels, dark wood. That is autumn wood.

steps.label: The annual ring and its significance
steps.margin_note: Write the word significance as a heading. The examiner looks for it.
lines: The spring wood and the autumn wood of one
year together form one ring.
In a transverse section of the trunk these
rings are seen one inside another, so they are
called annual rings.
One ring is added each year, so counting the
rings gives the approximate age of the tree.

lines.text: One annual ring = one year of growth

steps.why: A ring is visible only because the two kinds of wood look different, so the boundary between dark autumn wood and the next year's light spring wood marks one year. That is why counting works.
common_mistakes: Counting each light band and each dark band as a separate year. One ring is both together.
Giving the formation and forgetting the significance. The question asks for both.
steps.memory_tip: Light band plus the dark band that closes it is one year.

steps.label: Diagram of annual rings
steps.margin_note: Four or five circles are enough. Label bark, cork cambium and one annual ring.
steps.why: The rings only make sense as a picture: wide light bands closed by narrow dark bands, one pair for each year, with the bark outside.
common_mistakes: Drawing evenly spaced circles. The spring band is wide and the autumn band is narrow.
Leaving out the bark and the cork cambium, which the book labels.
steps.memory_tip: Draw a small centre, then wide circle, thin dark circle, wide circle, thin dark circle.

insider_note: The rings are only visible because the two woods differ, so the answer must explain the difference before it names the ring.
